judgments.brief_reason: The answer identifies the disabled content, its former location, and the URL or URLs to challenge.
It explicitly requires email address, name, telephone number, and physical address.
It includes the sworn, penalty-of-perjury statement of good-faith belief in mistake or misidentification.
It states the applicable federal jurisdiction rule and agreement to accept service of process.
It explicitly requires a physical or electronic signature.
It says contacting the user first is appreciated but not strictly required.
It limits the process to high-risk private information and says other removal requests cannot be processed simultaneously.
It explicitly warns that additional or multiple requests, including from additional contacts, may cause delays.
It identifies the contact form as the fastest submission option.
It praises plain-text email but does not say an attached submission must also include plain text in the email body.
It says plain-text email is much faster than physical mail, adequately conveying that physical mail takes substantially longer.
It explicitly says the 10–14 day period begins when GitHub receives the notice, not when sent.
It states that an authorized individual may request action regarding the deceased user's account.
It requires providing the requester's relationship to the deceased, including successor status.
It requires stating the desired action and gives repository transfer and billing cancellation as examples.
It says GitHub may request photo identification, a death certificate, and documentation of authority.
It expressly says posting other people's personal information is prohibited.
It states nonconsensual photos or videos may invade privacy, especially when presenting safety risks.
It explicitly says GitHub considers whether reported content is publicly available elsewhere.
It states that publicly available information shared to harass or incite abuse may violate the bullying and harassment prohibition.
